title: "Non-parametric tests"
subtitle: "Rank-based tests, rank correlation and permutation tests — and when you actually need them"
description: "Learn what rank-based tests do, run the Wilcoxon, Mann–Whitney, Kruskal–Wallis and Spearman tests in R, understand what hypotheses they really test, and use permutation tests as a flexible alternative."
---


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

:::



::: {.lesson-meta}
[Level 3 · Inference]{.level-3} [⏱ ~70 min]{} [Prerequisites: [t-tests](34-t-tests.qmd)]{}
:::

::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- explain what "non-parametric" and "rank-based" mean;
- run the **Wilcoxon signed-rank**, **Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann–Whitney)** and **Kruskal–Wallis** tests and follow up with adjusted pairwise comparisons;
- state what these tests actually test (and why it is not simply "the medians");
- compare **Pearson** and **Spearman** correlation tests with `cor.test()`;
- write a **permutation test** for any statistic, and decide when a non-parametric method is really needed.
:::




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```
:::


## 1. Why another family of tests?

The t-test of [t-tests](34-t-tests.qmd) compares **means** and uses the t distribution as its null distribution. That works well when samples are large or the data are roughly normal. It can work poorly when:

- samples are **small** *and* the data are clearly **skewed** or contain **outliers**: one extreme value can drag the mean and inflate the standard deviation;
- the data are **ordinal** — scores such as "1 = poor … 5 = excellent", where differences between categories are not equal distances, so a mean is hard to interpret.

**Non-parametric** methods make fewer assumptions about the shape of the distribution (they do not assume it belongs to a family described by a few *parameters*, such as the normal). The classical ones work on **ranks** instead of the raw values.

## 2. From values to ranks


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- c(3.1, 10, 2.5, 2.5, 7, 250)
rank(x)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 3.0 5.0 1.5 1.5 4.0 6.0
```


:::
:::


The smallest value gets rank 1, the next rank 2, and so on; tied values share the average of their ranks (the two 2.5's get 1.5 each). Notice the last value: whether it is 250 or 11, its rank is 6. **Ranks are insensitive to how extreme an outlier is** — this is where the robustness of rank tests comes from. The price is that some information about distances is thrown away.

## 3. Wilcoxon signed-rank test (one sample or paired)

The `sleep` data (used in [t-tests](34-t-tests.qmd)) give the extra hours of sleep for the same 10 patients under two drugs. The paired t-test works on the differences; the **signed-rank** test ranks the absolute differences and then compares the sum of ranks of the positive and the negative differences.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
drug1 <- sleep$extra[sleep$group == 1]
drug2 <- sleep$extra[sleep$group == 2]

wsr <- wilcox.test(drug2, drug1, paired = TRUE)
wsr
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> 
#> 	Wilcoxon signed rank exact test
#> 
#> data:  drug2 and drug1
#> V = 54, p-value = 0.004
#> alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
t.test(drug2, drug1, paired = TRUE)$p.value
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 0.002833
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- **V** is the sum of the ranks of the positive differences (54). Here 9 of the 10 patients slept more with drug 2 and one had no change, so the rank sum comes entirely from positive differences. (How zero differences are handled varies between methods; see `?wilcox.test`.)
- **p-value**: 0.0039. If the differences were symmetric around 0, a rank sum this lopsided would be rare.
- **"true location shift is not equal to 0"**: $H_0$ is that the differences are symmetric around 0.
- The paired t-test reaches the same conclusion. With clean data the two tests usually agree.
:::

For a single sample, `wilcox.test(x, mu = m0)` tests whether the distribution is symmetric around `m0`.

## 4. Wilcoxon rank-sum = Mann–Whitney test (two independent groups)

The `chickwts` data give the weight of chicks fed different diets. Compare *horsebean* with *linseed*:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
chicks2 <- chickwts |>
  filter(feed %in% c("horsebean", "linseed")) |>
  droplevels()

tapply(chicks2$weight, chicks2$feed, median)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> horsebean   linseed 
#>     151.5     221.0
```


:::
:::


The **rank-sum** test pools the two groups, ranks all observations together and checks whether one group's ranks are systematically higher. The same test is known as the **Mann–Whitney U** test.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
mw <- wilcox.test(weight ~ feed, data = chicks2, conf.int = TRUE)
mw
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> 
#> 	Wilcoxon rank sum exact test
#> 
#> data:  weight by feed
#> W = 20, p-value = 0.007
#> alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0
#> 96 percent confidence interval:
#>  -105  -12
#> sample estimates:
#> difference in location 
#>                  -60.5
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- **W** = 20 counts, over all 120 horsebean–linseed pairs, how many times the horsebean chick is heavier. So $W / (n_1 n_2)$ = 0.17 estimates **$P(\text{horsebean} > \text{linseed})$**. Under $H_0$ this probability would be 0.5.
- **p-value** 0.0071: horsebean chicks tend to be lighter.
- **difference in location** (-60.5 g) with its CI (for exact tests R reports the achievable confidence level, which can be slightly above 95%): the *Hodges–Lehmann* estimate, the median of all pairwise differences. It is a sensible summary of the shift **if** the two distributions have the same shape.
:::

### What does the rank-sum test really test?

It is often said that the Mann–Whitney test "compares medians". That is only true under an extra assumption: that the two distributions have **the same shape** and differ only by a shift. In general, it tests whether **one group tends to produce larger values than the other**, i.e. whether $P(X > Y) \neq 0.5$ (*stochastic dominance*).

A simulation makes the difference visible. Below, both groups have **exactly the same median (0)**, but one is skewed to the right and the other to the left:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(10)
reject <- replicate(2000, {
  x <- rexp(100) - log(2)       # median 0, long right tail
  y <- -(rexp(100) - log(2))    # median 0, long left tail
  wilcox.test(x, y)$p.value < 0.05
})
mean(reject)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 0.6675
```


:::
:::


The test rejects in 67% of the samples, although the medians are equal. It is not wrong: $X$ really does tend to be larger than $Y$. It just does not answer a question about medians. **Say "the values in group A tend to be larger", not "the medians differ"**, unless the shapes look similar.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: the statistics

- **Signed-rank:** rank $|d_i|$ for the non-zero differences; $V = \sum_{d_i > 0} \text{rank}(|d_i|)$. Under $H_0$ each sign is + or − with probability 1/2, so the null distribution of $V$ can be enumerated exactly (small $n$) or approximated by a normal.
- **Rank-sum:** $W = \sum_{i}\sum_{j} \mathbf 1(x_i > y_j)$ (ties count 1/2). This is R's $W$; it equals the sum of the ranks of the first sample minus $n_1(n_1+1)/2$. Under $H_0$ (same distribution), $E[W] = n_1 n_2 / 2$.
- **Efficiency:** for normal data, rank tests lose little: their asymptotic relative efficiency compared with the t-test is $3/\pi \approx 0.955$. For heavy-tailed data they can be far more powerful than the t-test.
:::

## 5. Kruskal–Wallis test (three or more groups)

The rank-based version of one-way ANOVA (see [ANOVA](37-anova.qmd)): are all groups drawn from the same distribution?


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(chickwts, aes(reorder(feed, weight, FUN = median), weight)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Feed (ordered by median weight)", y = "Weight (g)")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Chick weight by feed type (71 chicks, six diets).](36-nonparametric-tests_files/figure-html/fig-chickwts-1.png){#fig-chickwts fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
kw <- kruskal.test(weight ~ feed, data = chickwts)
kw
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> 
#> 	Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test
#> 
#> data:  weight by feed
#> Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 37, df = 5, p-value = 5e-07
```


:::
:::


The p-value (5.1e-07) says that at least one feed differs from the others. To see **which pairs** differ, use pairwise rank-sum tests with a multiple-testing adjustment (see [Hypothesis testing](33-hypothesis-testing.qmd)):


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
pairwise.wilcox.test(chickwts$weight, chickwts$feed,
                     p.adjust.method = "holm", exact = FALSE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> 
#> 	Pairwise comparisons using Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction 
#> 
#> data:  chickwts$weight and chickwts$feed 
#> 
#>           casein horsebean linseed meatmeal soybean
#> horsebean 0.003  -         -       -        -      
#> linseed   0.012  0.064     -       -        -      
#> meatmeal  0.362  0.009     0.218   -        -      
#> soybean   0.047  0.009     0.710   0.710    -      
#> sunflower 1.000  0.002     0.003   0.347    0.014  
#> 
#> P value adjustment method: holm
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

Each cell is a Holm-adjusted p-value for one pair of feeds. For example, *horsebean* differs from *casein* and *sunflower* (adjusted p well below 0.01), while *casein* and *sunflower* are indistinguishable. `exact = FALSE` uses the normal approximation, which avoids warnings when there are ties.
:::

## 6. Correlation: Pearson and Spearman side by side

`cor.test()` tests $H_0$: "no correlation". The **Pearson** correlation measures *linear* association; the **Spearman** correlation is the Pearson correlation of the **ranks**, so it measures *monotonic* association (one variable tends to increase with the other, not necessarily in a straight line). See [Correlation](../06-visualization/27-correlation.qmd) for the descriptive side.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
pear <- cor.test(~ Ozone + Temp, data = airquality)
spear <- cor.test(~ Ozone + Temp, data = airquality,
                  method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
c(pearson = unname(pear$estimate), spearman = unname(spear$estimate))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>  pearson spearman 
#>   0.6984   0.7740
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
c(pearson = pear$p.value, spearman = spear$p.value)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>   pearson  spearman 
#> 2.932e-18 2.248e-24
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
pear$conf.int
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 0.5913 0.7812
#> attr(,"conf.level")
#> [1] 0.95
```


:::
:::


Both indicate a strong positive association between temperature and ozone. Spearman's $\rho$ (0.77) is a bit higher than Pearson's $r$ (0.7) because the relationship curves upwards: it is monotonic but not linear. Only the Pearson test provides a confidence interval in `cor.test()`.

The difference is dramatic when there is an **outlier**:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(4)
x <- 1:20
y <- x + rnorm(20, sd = 3)
y[20] <- -40                      # one wild value
c(pearson  = cor(x, y),
  spearman = cor(x, y, method = "spearman"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>  pearson spearman 
#>  0.04455  0.63759
```


:::
:::


A single point destroys the Pearson correlation (it falls to 0.04), while Spearman's ($\rho =$ 0.64) still sees the clear increasing trend in the other 19 points. Always **plot** before you correlate.

## 7. Permutation tests: a flexible alternative

The permutation test of [Hypothesis testing](33-hypothesis-testing.qmd) works with **any** statistic you choose. Suppose you really care about the **difference in medians** between horsebean and linseed chicks:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
med_diff <- function(y, g) {
  m <- tapply(y, g, median)
  unname(m["linseed"] - m["horsebean"])
}
obs <- med_diff(chicks2$weight, chicks2$feed)

set.seed(1)
perm <- replicate(10000, med_diff(chicks2$weight, sample(chicks2$feed)))
p_perm <- mean(abs(perm) >= abs(obs))
c(observed = obs, p_value = p_perm)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> observed  p_value 
#>  69.5000   0.0228
```


:::
:::


The observed difference in medians is 69.5 g, and only 2.3% of the shuffled datasets produce one at least as large. The recipe is always the same: **choose a statistic → shuffle under $H_0$ → compare**. It works for medians, trimmed means, ratios of variances, correlations, and more. Two requirements: under $H_0$ the shuffled labels must be exchangeable (for example, independent units), and the shuffle must respect the design (for paired data, swap the values *within* each pair, rather than shuffling freely).

## 8. When to use what

| Situation | Parametric | Rank-based | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| One sample or paired differences | `t.test(x, mu = )`, `t.test(..., paired = TRUE)` | `wilcox.test(x, mu = )`, `wilcox.test(..., paired = TRUE)` | Signed-rank assumes symmetric differences |
| Two independent groups | `t.test(y ~ g)` (Welch) | `wilcox.test(y ~ g)` | Rank-sum tests $P(X > Y) = 0.5$ |
| Three or more groups | `aov()`, `oneway.test()` | `kruskal.test()` + `pairwise.wilcox.test()` | See [ANOVA](37-anova.qmd) |
| Association of two numeric variables | `cor.test()` (Pearson) | `cor.test(method = "spearman")` | Spearman: monotonic, robust to outliers |
| Any statistic, any design | — | Permutation test | Shuffle according to the design |

### "My data aren't normal" is not automatically a reason to switch

- **With moderate or large samples**, the t-test is robust: it is about the *sampling distribution of the mean*, which the Central Limit Theorem makes approximately normal (see [Sampling distributions](../07-probability/30-sampling-distributions.qmd)). Welch's test also handles unequal variances.
- **The tests answer different questions.** The t-test is about means; the rank-sum test is about $P(X > Y)$. If the mean is what matters (total cost, total yield), a rank test answers the wrong question.
- **A formal normality test is a poor guide**: with small samples it rarely detects non-normality, with large ones it flags harmless deviations. Look at plots and think about the data.
- **Other options exist**: a transformation (for example, the logarithm for right-skewed positive data), a bootstrap CI ([Bootstrap](../07-probability/31-bootstrap.qmd)), or a permutation test of the mean.
- **Rank tests are a good choice** for small samples with outliers or strong skew, for ordinal data, and when "tends to be larger" is the natural question.

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Saying "the medians differ" after a Mann–Whitney test.** That is only justified if the distributions have similar shapes.
2. **Thinking non-parametric means assumption-free.** Rank tests still assume independent observations; the signed-rank test assumes symmetric differences.
3. **Switching tests after seeing which one gives the smaller p-value.** Choose the test from the question and the design, before the analysis.
4. **Using the rank-sum test on paired data** (or the signed-rank test on independent groups). As with t-tests, the design decides.
5. **Forgetting the multiple-comparison adjustment** after a significant Kruskal–Wallis test.
6. **Reporting only a p-value.** Report an effect too: the Hodges–Lehmann shift with its CI, $P(X > Y)$, or Spearman's $\rho$.
:::

## 9. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. Why is a rank test hardly affected by one extremely large value?

Because the largest value gets the largest rank whatever its size: replacing 250 by 2,500 does not change any rank.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. A Mann–Whitney test gives W = 90 with n1 = 10 and n2 = 12. What does W / (n1·n2) estimate, and what is its value under H0?

It estimates $P(X > Y)$, the probability that a random observation from group 1 exceeds one from group 2: here 90/120 = 0.75. Under $H_0$ it would be 0.5.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. Pearson r = 0.05 and Spearman ρ = 0.64 on the same data. What would you suspect?

An outlier (or a strongly non-linear but monotonic relation) is hiding the association from Pearson's r. Plot the data.
:::

## 10. Exercises

### Interactive (run in your browser)

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — two independent groups.** Compare `mpg` between automatic (`am == 0`) and manual (`am == 1`) cars in `mtcars` with a rank-sum test, and with a Welch t-test. Do they agree?


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_36_1'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_36_1
wilcox.test(______ ~ ______, data = mtcars)
t.test(mpg ~ am, data = mtcars)$p.value
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_36_1"}
The formula is `outcome ~ group`, as in `t.test()`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_36_1"}
```r
wilcox.test(mpg ~ am, data = mtcars)
```
Both tests find a clear difference (p about 0.001 for both the rank-sum test and Welch): manual cars tend to have higher `mpg`. With clear effects and reasonably shaped data, the two approaches agree.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — Kruskal–Wallis and follow-up.** The `InsectSprays` data give insect counts on plots treated with six sprays (A–F). Counts are skewed and the variances differ a lot between sprays. Run a Kruskal–Wallis test and the Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons. Which sprays seem most effective (lowest counts)?


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_36_2'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_36_2
tapply(InsectSprays$count, InsectSprays$spray, median)
kruskal.test(______ ~ ______, data = InsectSprays)
pairwise.wilcox.test(InsectSprays$count, InsectSprays$spray,
                     p.adjust.method = "______", exact = FALSE)
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_36_2"}
The outcome is `count` and the group is `spray`; the adjustment method is `"holm"`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_36_2"}
```r
kruskal.test(count ~ spray, data = InsectSprays)
pairwise.wilcox.test(InsectSprays$count, InsectSprays$spray,
                     p.adjust.method = "holm", exact = FALSE)
```
The Kruskal–Wallis test is highly significant. Sprays **C, D and E** have the lowest medians, and each of them differs from A, B and F (adjusted p < 0.001). Among C, D and E, only C vs D reaches significance (about 0.016).
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — an outlier and two correlations.** Run the code and compare the Pearson and Spearman tests. Then remove the outlier (`x[-20]`, `y[-20]`) and repeat the Pearson test. What changes?


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_36_3'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_36_3
set.seed(4)
x <- 1:20
y <- x + rnorm(20, sd = 3)
y[20] <- -40
cor.test(x, y)$p.value
cor.test(x, y, method = "______")$p.value
cor.test(x[______], y[______])$estimate
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_36_3"}
Use `method = "spearman"`, and `-20` to drop the 20th element.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_36_3"}
```r
cor.test(x, y)$p.value                        # about 0.85
cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman")$p.value   # about 0.003
cor.test(x[-20], y[-20])$estimate             # about 0.9
```
With the outlier, Pearson sees no association; Spearman detects the trend. Without the outlier, Pearson's r is high again. Never delete points just to obtain a result — but always investigate them: is it a data-entry error, or a real and interesting observation?
:::
:::

### Practice on your own computer

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — a permutation test for paired data.** For the `sleep` data, write a permutation test of the **mean paired difference** (drug 2 − drug 1). Under $H_0$ each difference is equally likely to be positive or negative, so randomly flip the signs of the differences instead of shuffling labels. Compare with the paired t-test.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
d <- sleep$extra[sleep$group == 2] - sleep$extra[sleep$group == 1]
obs <- mean(d)

set.seed(1)
perm <- replicate(10000, {
  signs <- sample(c(-1, 1), length(d), replace = TRUE)
  mean(signs * d)
})
mean(abs(perm) >= abs(obs))
t.test(d)$p.value
```
The sign-flip p-value is close to the paired t-test p-value (both well below 0.01: about 0.004 and 0.003). Shuffling freely between the two groups would break the pairing — the permutation must follow the design.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — choose the test.** For each situation, name a suitable test and say why. (a) Pain scores (0–10) for 12 patients before and after physiotherapy. (b) Income of 800 men and 800 women, very right-skewed; the question is about average income. (c) Satisfaction ratings (1–5) for four different help-desk teams.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) Paired ordinal data with small $n$: **Wilcoxon signed-rank** (`paired = TRUE`). (b) The question is about **means** and $n$ is large: **Welch t-test** (the CLT applies); a bootstrap CI for the difference in means, or an analysis on the log scale (which compares geometric means), are good complements. A rank test would answer a different question. (c) Ordinal outcome, four independent groups: **Kruskal–Wallis**, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise Wilcoxon tests.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Test | R | Tests whether… |
|---|---|---|
| Signed-rank | `wilcox.test(x, mu = )` / `wilcox.test(a, b, paired = TRUE)` | (differences) are symmetric around the reference |
| Rank-sum / Mann–Whitney | `wilcox.test(y ~ g, conf.int = TRUE)` | one group tends to give larger values ($P(X>Y) \ne 0.5$) |
| Kruskal–Wallis | `kruskal.test(y ~ g)` + `pairwise.wilcox.test()` | all groups come from the same distribution |
| Pearson / Spearman | `cor.test(x, y)` / `cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman")` | linear / monotonic association |
| Permutation | `replicate()` + `sample()` | any statistic you choose is larger than chance would give |

- Rank tests replace values by ranks: robust to outliers, suitable for ordinal data.
- The rank-sum test is **not** a test of medians unless the shapes are equal.
- Spearman is Pearson on ranks: it captures monotonic trends and resists outliers.
- Permutation tests are flexible; shuffle in a way that respects the design.
- Non-normal data with a decent sample size do not automatically require a non-parametric test — think about the question first.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
